summary: A speculative theory analyzing the January 2021 GameStop trading halt through the lens of Regulation SHO settlement obligations. The author proposes that Robinhood halted trading on January 28 because Citadel had failed to deliver shares beyond the 35-day settlement threshold, making Robinhood liable. The central thesis holds that Citadel deliberately orchestrated a scenario where other brokers would face the squeeze instead, and that the "MOASS" is delayed while regulators secretly coordinate to prevent Citadel from avoiding squeeze liability. The work correctly describes settlement mechanics and regulatory provisions but relies heavily on unverified inference, treating speculative conclusions as derivations from timing coincidence.

key_claims.claim: Claims that GME was on the threshold list for 39 consecutive settlement days from early December to early February, with Robinhood halting trading on January 28, which is day 35 of this streak
key_claims.note: Timing claim is specific and corresponds to documented threshold-list data; author references detailed prior analysis (pages 3-4)

key_claims.claim: Claims that the MOASS (Mother of All Short Squeezes) will eventually occur once new regulations ensure Citadel is squeezed rather than other market participants
key_claims.note: Prediction deadline has long passed (work pub. Aug 2021; hindsight date Sept 2026). No MOASS occurred; GME peaked ~$65 May-June 2024, not price-spike trajectory implied

key_claims.claim: Claims that Citadel deliberately engineered a scenario where its failed deliveries would force other brokers (esp. Robinhood) to be squeezed first, making Citadel protected from margin-call risk
key_claims.note: SEC Oct 2021 staff report found the Jan 2021 run-up was driven mainly by retail positive-sentiment buying, NOT by short covering or deliberate orchestration. No evidence supports Citadel's deliberate market manipulation here

key_claims.claim: Claims that Robinhood halted trading because Citadel had failed to deliver GME shares, crossing the 35-day SHO settlement threshold and making Robinhood liable to its customers
key_claims.note: The SHO § 242.203(b2) settlement mechanism is real and accurately described (pages 3-4). The claim that Citadel specifically failed to deliver to Robinhood is unproven; author infers it from timing alignment but provides no direct evidence of actual FTD data

key_claims.claim: Claims that Citadel maintains privilege and exemptions as a market maker that shield it from immediate squeeze liability compared to retail brokers
key_claims.note: Consistent with hindsight: Citadel Securities remains major market maker; Citadel was never margin-called into collapse despite widespread predictions

key_claims.claim: Claims that the SEC and DTCC regulators are coordinating behind the scenes to update regulations to prevent Citadel from forcing others to be squeezed before Citadel itself
key_claims.note: Unfalsifiable claim about behind-the-scenes negotiation. Citadel remains operational as of 2026 with no systemic squeeze threat, consistent with continued normal operation rather than impending 'destruction'

validity_rationale: The central prediction (MOASS will eventually occur) has definitively failed as of 2026. The core theory — that Citadel deliberately orchestrated failed deliveries to force other brokers to be squeezed first — is pure speculation contradicted by the SEC's Oct 2021 finding that retail sentiment, not short covering, drove the price. While the author accurately describes settlement mechanics under Regulation SHO, the inference that Citadel specifically failed to deliver to Robinhood is unsupported by data. Some ancillary claims align with hindsight (Citadel avoided margin-call, trading halt did occur and end the spike), but these do not validate the mechanism proposed. The work's own disclaimer ("tinfoil hat," "random on the internet spinning yarns") signals awareness of low evidentiary standard.
